title: Penance as service
hookLine: penance is often seva: cleaning shoes, washing dishes, reading bani

lines: THE SHOE HOUSE BY THE DOOR.
A JOB BY THE FRONT DOOR.
cards: Near the door of a gurdwara there's often a counter with rows of shoes on shelves. You hand over your sneakers, someone gives you a token, and when you leave the same hands give them back, sometimes wiped clean.

Sikhs call it the joda ghar, the shoe house. Now suppose the person behind that counter today is there because of a mistake. The five set a tankhah, and this is it: a week of handling other people's shoes.
Not a fine paid at an office. Not a ban from the building. A job, right by the front door, where everybody walks in.

teach.b: When five Sikhs set a tankhah, the penance is often seva, selfless service, and the Sikh Rehat Maryada leans that way too: in paraphrase, it asks that the penance take the form of service, preferably work done with the hands.

So a tankhah can look like cleaning shoes in the joda ghar, washing dishes in the langar after the meal, sweeping the floor, fetching water, or reciting a set portion of bani, the Guru's words, daily for a time.
Turn that over a few ways.

teach.h: KEPT IN THE MIDDLE, NOT PUSHED OUT.
teach.b: First, the penance keeps the person in the middle of the sangat. A ban pushes someone out; a shoe counter puts them by the door, greeting everyone who comes in.
The mistake cut them off a little; the service stitches them back. Second, it's humble work, and meant to be. The shoe house and the dish pile are where pride has nowhere to stand.
And because volunteers do the same seva with no penance at all, from the outside the penitent looks like any other volunteer.

teach.h: THE HANDS THAT BROKE IT MEND IT.
teach.b: Third, the hands that broke the promise get to do something good. A wrong isn't undone by feeling bad for long enough; it's answered by work for others, in the open, until the five's term is done.
And fourth, the bani. When the penance is recitation, the Guru's words do the mending, morning after morning, in the person's own mouth. Shoes, dishes, words.

how: A tankhah set by five Sikhs is often a form of seva, such as cleaning shoes at the joda ghar, washing dishes in the langar, or reciting set portions of bani for a period.

o: a penance served as humble work, like shoes or dishes
volunteering at the gurdwara to earn a higher rank
a donation paid in place of attending prayers

games.q: penance as service: tap the pairs.
p: the shoe house by the gurdwara door
the Guru's words, recited as penance

s: a tankhah is a fine paid to the gurdwara
it is often seva: shoes, dishes, sweeping, or reciting bani.
the code leans toward penance done with the hands
it asks that the penance take the form of service, preferably physical work.
you can spot the person doing penance at the sink
volunteers do the same seva with no penance, so the penitent looks like any volunteer.

games.q: you're one of the five, setting a tankhah for someone who broke the code. what do you choose?
o: a fine, paid to the committee.
a time of seva: shoes, dishes, or reciting bani.
a ban from the gurdwara for a year.
games.why: the code leans toward service. it keeps the person in the middle of the sangat, doing humble work, instead of pushing them out.

practice: If you can, get up and do one small job nobody will thank you for, wiping a counter, lining up the shoes by the door, washing the one cup in the sink, and move slowly, giving it your whole attention.
If you can't move right now, picture every step of it instead, then sit quietly with what your hands did.

wordCard.voice: Penance as service. A tankhah often takes the form of seva: shoes, dishes, sweeping or recited bani, done in the open among the sangat. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: selfless service. a tankhah is often set as seva.

carryVoice: Your line: mended by service. A wrong is answered by work for others. See you tomorrow.
